In films, the villain is always a brilliant [[psychopath]] with a chilling smile, but her professor said real cases are usually far less glamorous. He explained that a [[sociopath]], by contrast, tends to be impulsive and quick to anger rather than coldly calculating. Another myth is the villain pressing a cloth soaked in [[chloroform]] over someone's face, since in reality it takes minutes to work and could easily kill the victim. The lecture Ira found most useful was about everyday dangers like [[stalking]], which often begins with someone constantly checking a person's social media and turning up wherever they go. Her professor stressed that an [[abuser]] is usually someone the victim already knows, and that a [[pedophile]] may pretend to be a friendly teenager online to gain a child's trust. The class had even discussed why [[incest]] is a crime in almost every legal system, and why [[cannibalism]], which shocks us so deeply, actually occurs among some animals when food runs out. Lisa admitted that after so many thrillers, she sometimes felt a touch of [[paranoia]] when walking home alone at night. Ira smiled and said the course had actually made her calmer, because knowing the real warning signs is far better than being afraid of everything.

lessons.title: An army on the move
lessons.story: On Saturday, Anna took her little brother Taras to the military history museum, where their grandfather volunteers as a guide. The first hall was devoted to ancient Rome, and Grandpa explained that a [[centurion]] commanded about a hundred soldiers and fought in the front row himself. In the next room, Taras pressed his nose against a model of an enormous [[armada]] of wooden warships sailing toward an enemy coast. Grandpa, who had served in the navy for thirty years, admitted that he had never become an [[admiral]], but he joked that he had once brought one a cup of coffee. He showed them a photo of himself as an eighteen-year-old [[cadet]], so thin that his uniform looked two sizes too big. Back then, every new [[recruit]] had to practice the same difficult [[maneuver]] for bringing a ship into port during a storm. The last hall told the story of a [[battalion]] that had protected a [[convoy]] of trucks carrying food to a city under siege, and a quiet display honored the [[heroism]] of the drivers. Next to it, a map showed how several countries built up a nuclear [[arsenal]] during the Cold War. On the way home, Taras announced that he was going to join the navy, and Grandpa promised to teach him sailor's knots first.

lessons.title: Checking a conflict report
lessons.story: Anna spent Saturday fact-checking a draft report for her journalism professor in Kyiv. The writer had called one fighter's pistol a [[magnum]], but the photo clearly showed a small-[[caliber]] handgun. A paragraph about a bridge fire claimed [[sabotage]], and the police had in fact recovered a [[detonator]] near the rails. Max, reading over her shoulder, asked why the report used so many different labels for armed groups. Anna explained that an [[insurgent]] fights against a government, while a [[separatist]] wants a region to break away. She added that calling someone a [[jihadist]] is a serious claim, and that the word [[jihad]] itself originally means "struggle." The trickiest sentence named one state as the [[aggressor]], so she checked it against three independent sources before leaving it in. By evening, her notes were longer than the report, and the professor thanked her for catching every slip.

lessons.title: Genes and mutants
lessons.story: Taras came home excited about a movie in which a [[mutant]] could change the color of his skin at will. Anna, who had a genetics exam on Monday, decided to turn his question into a study break. She explained that skin color depends mostly on a [[pigment]] called melanin, and that cells need a special [[enzyme]] to produce it. "So is the secret hidden somewhere in his [[genome]]?" Taras asked. Partly, she said, but a cell also needs the right [[receptor]] to catch the signal that switches production on. Max's sister Sofia, who was doing an internship at a [[biotech]] startup, joined the video call and confirmed that real science moves much more slowly than the movies. Taras looked disappointed for a moment, then announced that he would become a scientist and speed things up.

lessons.title: Inside the atom
lessons.story: Anna's grandfather, a retired engineer, took her and Taras to the science museum on a rainy Sunday. In the first hall, a glowing model showed a single [[proton]] at the center of a [[hydrogen]] atom. Taras pressed a button, and the model added a [[neutron]], turning the atom into a heavier [[isotope]] called deuterium. "And what's inside those little balls?" he asked, so Grandpa pointed to a screen where each [[quark]] appeared as a tiny colored dot. Next came a glass ball full of [[plasma]], where purple threads followed Taras's fingers across the surface. Grandpa explained that electricity had pulled electrons away, turning the gas atoms inside into [[ions|ion]]. In the last room, a model of a nuclear [[reactor]] showed how much of the country's power is produced. Before leaving, Taras caught a single [[photon]] on a light detector, and the counter clicked once. On the way home, he declared that atoms were cooler than dinosaurs, and Grandpa smiled as if he had finally won a long argument.

lessons.title: In the electricity lab
lessons.story: In Thursday's lab session, Anna and Max had to build a simple circuit and measure everything carefully. First, Max checked the [[voltage]] of their battery, which read just under nine [[volts|volt]]. Anna added a resistor of two hundred [[ohms|ohm]] and reminded him that the professor wanted every value written in [[SI]] units. For the next step, they drew a thick line with a soft pencil, because [[graphite]] conducts electricity surprisingly well. A small green [[indicator]] lit up the moment the current passed through the drawing. Their table also held samples of [[nickel]], [[cobalt]], and [[chrome]], and they had to find out which ones a magnet would pick up. Finally, the professor struck a tuning fork next to a second one, and [[resonance]] made the second fork hum on its own. Max was so pleased that he hummed along, and Anna described it in the report as an unplanned experiment.

lessons.title: In the chemistry lab
lessons.story: On her first day as a lab assistant, Anna got a tour of the chemistry stockroom from her friend Ira, who had worked there for a year. Ira began with safety: everyone wears [[latex]] gloves, and people who are allergic will find nitrile ones in the second drawer. The locked cabinet held [[cyanide]], which no student was allowed to touch without a supervisor. On the open shelves stood jars of iron [[oxide]], a bag of sodium [[chloride]], and fertilizer samples rich in [[nitrate]] and [[phosphate]]. Near the window, a bottle of [[ethanol]] was kept for cleaning equipment, next to an old brown bottle of [[ether]] from the 1970s. Ira then opened a drawer of plastic samples and explained that each one was a different [[polymer]]. The last item was a set of [[silicone]] molds, which, Ira admitted, were not for science at all but for the lab's monthly cake day. Anna laughed and decided that this was going to be a very good job.

lessons.title: A poster about space
lessons.story: Anna and Max spent the evening designing a poster for the university's astronomy night. Max painted the background as a dark [[gradient]], from deep blue at the bottom to black at the top. In the center, Anna placed a chart of the night sky divided into four parts and put the brightest star in the upper left [[quadrant]]. Next to it, she drew a [[vector]] to show the direction and speed of a passing comet. Max insisted on adding the comet's orbit equation, even though few visitors would check whether the [[coefficient]] in front of x was right. Their main text described the [[genesis]] of the [[cosmos]], based on a simulation the physics department had run on a computer [[cluster]] for weeks. A small box explained why the sun reaches its [[zenith]] much higher over Kyiv in June than in December. When Max complained that constellations were just a human [[construct]], Anna pointed out a clear [[parallel]] with borders on a map: invented, but still useful. The poster won second place, and the prize was a pizza, which Max called the true center of the universe.

lessons.title: Kings, dukes, and nobles
lessons.story: Lisa came over to study for their European history exam, and Anna's little brother Taras insisted on helping. He took the flashcards and began with the easiest question: who ranks higher, a [[duke]] or a [[baron]]? Lisa answered correctly, then added that in England an [[earl]] sits between the two. The next card asked what a [[regent]] does, and Anna explained that one rules while the [[monarch]] is still a child. Taras liked the word [[kaiser]] so much that he started using it as a nickname for the family cat. Lisa explained that the [[gentry]] owned land but usually had no titles, unlike a true [[aristocrat]]. The last card said only "[[sovereign]]," and Anna said it was a formal word for a king or queen who holds supreme power. By midnight, the cat was wearing a paper crown, and the girls felt ready for anything the exam might bring.

lessons.title: Empires of the East
lessons.story: Anna took her grandmother to a new exhibition about the empires of the East at the history museum. The first room showed a map of a vast [[caliphate]] that once stretched from Spain to Central Asia. Next came a model of a [[sultan]]'s palace, including the private quarters known as the [[harem]], where his wives and children lived. Grandma admitted that she had always pictured the [[steppe]] as endless grass, and the huge photos proved her right. In a corner, a stuffed [[yak]] reminded visitors how people crossed cold mountain passes with heavy loads. The final hall was dedicated to a stone [[citadel]] on a hill that had served as the last [[bastion]] against invaders for two centuries. On the way out, Grandma bought a postcard of a shaggy mountain animal for Taras, who would certainly want to ride one.

lessons.title: Life on the frontier
lessons.story: On Saturday, Anna and Max visited a small museum about life on the American [[frontier]]. The first room told the story of a [[pioneer]] family who crossed the plains in a wooden wagon. Next to it, a map showed where each [[colonist]] had settled along the river. Max was fascinated by a fur coat that once belonged to a [[trapper]] who spent whole winters alone in the woods. In the next hall, the museum had rebuilt an old [[saloon]], complete with a piano and swinging doors. A guide explained that news from the East used to arrive by [[telegraph]], often days after the events. Anna's favorite display was a poster for a traveling [[charlatan]] who promised to cure everything from headaches to heartbreak. He sold a bright green [[elixir]] that, according to the label, was mostly sugar and alcohol. "Real help came from the local [[healer]], who knew which plants actually worked," the guide added. On the way home, Max joked that his grandmother's herbal tea was the only miracle cure he trusted.

lessons.title: Dark times in history
lessons.story: Anna's grandfather came to her university to give a talk about the darkest chapters of the twentieth century. He began by explaining how [[fascism]] grew out of fear, poverty, and anger after the First World War. In Germany, the [[national socialists|national socialist]] used propaganda and violence to crush any opposition. He showed a photo of an ancient Indian temple to point out that the [[swastika]] had been a peaceful symbol for thousands of years before it was stolen. Then his voice grew quieter as he spoke about the [[genocide]] of the Holocaust and the millions of lives it took. A student asked whether these regimes were the only danger, and he replied that [[imperialism]] had also caused enormous suffering across the world. He added that in some countries, a military [[junta]] later seized power and silenced journalists for years. At the end, he told the students that remembering history is the best way to protect democracy. Anna felt proud of him as the room filled with applause.

lessons.title: Church and faith
lessons.story: Ira invited Anna to a lecture on the history of Christianity at the city library. The speaker began with the Middle Ages, when a powerful [[inquisitor]] could put anyone on trial for their beliefs. She showed a portrait of a [[cardinal]] in scarlet robes, painted in Rome in the sixteenth century. Then she described daily life in a monastery, where the [[abbot]] made every important decision. Serious disagreements were settled at a [[synod]], where church leaders sometimes argued for weeks. Ira, who was raised a [[Protestant]], asked how the Reformation changed the relationship with [[Catholicism]]. The speaker explained that the reformers kept only two of the seven rituals, and that baptism remained a [[sacrament]] for almost everyone. She also mentioned later movements, such as the [[Baptist]] churches in England and the [[Mormon]] community that eventually settled in Utah. Afterward, Anna noticed a small wooden [[crucifix]] above the library door and wondered how long it had hung there. Ira laughed and said it had probably outlived several librarians.

lessons.title: Faiths of the world
lessons.story: For her world religions course, Anna had to interview people of different faiths. First, she visited a mosque in Kyiv, where a friendly [[imam]] explained how Friday prayers are organized. He mentioned that in some countries a religious teacher is called a [[mullah]], and that the word [[cleric]] covers many different roles. When Anna asked about the news, he said calmly that an [[Islamist]] political movement does not speak for most Muslims. The next weekend, Anna and Lisa went on a meditation [[retreat]] in the Carpathian Mountains. Their teacher had studied for years with a Tibetan [[lama]] and spoke softly about letting go of desire. According to Buddhism, he said, this path eventually leads to [[nirvana]]. Lisa was more interested in the yoga class, where the instructor talked about balancing each [[chakra]] and the idea of [[yin]] and yang. By Sunday evening, Anna had a notebook full of interviews and a new [[mantra]]: "One deadline at a time."

lessons.title: Myths and magic
lessons.story: Sofia threw a costume party with one rule: everyone had to dress as a creature or figure from world folklore. Max arrived as a [[ghoul]], with gray face paint and a torn jacket that frightened the neighbor's cat. Lisa chose a cheerful Irish [[leprechaun]], complete with a green hat and a pot of chocolate coins. Ira went for something darker and played a [[banshee]], wailing dramatically every time someone opened the door. Anna came as a [[jinn]] from the Arabian Nights, wrapped in blue silk and carrying a brass lamp. Taras wore a long white robe and a fake beard, insisting he was a Celtic [[druid]] and not a wizard. Sofia herself dressed as a Siberian [[shaman]] with a painted drum. Later, someone asked about [[voodoo]], and Ira explained that it is a real religion, not just a horror-movie cliché. The prize for best costume went to Taras, who had also carved a tiny [[totem]] out of a carrot. He wore a cardboard [[amulet]] around his neck and claimed it gave him a winning [[aura]].

lessons.title: The end of the world
lessons.story: On Friday night, Anna and Max went to a film club that was showing an old thriller about the end of the world. In the story, a quiet village believes a young stranger is the [[messiah]], until strange things begin to happen. Soon the local priest becomes convinced that the boy is actually the [[antichrist]]. In one striking scene, a stained-glass window of an [[archangel]] shatters during a storm. By the final act, the whole town is preparing for [[armageddon]]. During the discussion afterward, an older man argued that the film criticized blind [[dogma]] rather than religion itself. A student replied that it seemed closer to [[atheism]], since no miracle ever saves the characters. Max said the ending, with its empty church and ringing bells, was a complete [[enigma]] to him. Anna smiled and suggested they watch a comedy next week.

exclamations.title: Hey, mhm, pardon?
exclamations.story:
Anna: [[Hey|hey]], Max!
Max: [[Yo|yo]], Anna! What's up?
Anna: Let's go to the cinema tonight.
Max: [[Mhm|mhm]]. Which film?
Anna: [[Hmm|hmm]], maybe the funny one.
Max: [[Pardon|pardon]]? The line is bad.
Anna: The funny film! At six.
Max: [[Okey-dokey|okey-dokey]]. See you at six.
Anna: [[Bye|bye]]!

exclamations.title: Wow, Max's New Flat!
exclamations.story:
Max: Come in, Anna! This is my new flat.
Anna: [[Wow|wow]]! Look at the view from this window!
Max: Thanks. And this is my new lamp.
Anna: [[Ah|ah]], it looks like a big orange fish. [[Huh|huh]]? Does it really work?
Max: Yes, it does! Now look at my new jacket.
Anna: [[Oho|oho]], very nice! [[Ooh la la|ooh la la]], you look like a movie star!
Max: Now come into the kitchen.
Anna: [[OMG]], what a mess! [[Caramba|caramba]], are those old pizza boxes?
Max: Sorry! But [[voila]], my fridge is full of juice.
Max: Wait, what is under this box? [[Eureka|eureka]]! My lost keys!
Anna: Great! Now let's clean this kitchen together.

exclamations.title: Oops! A Bad Morning
exclamations.story:
Taras: [[Oops|oops]]! I dropped my phone in the hall.
Mama: Is it OK, Taras?
Taras: Yes, it's fine. [[Brr|brr]], the bathroom is so cold this morning!
Mama: Sorry, the heater is broken. Come and eat your soup.
Taras: [[Feh|feh]], the soup is cold too.
Grandpa: [[Fie|fie]] on this cold house! I sound like an old king in a film.
Anna: [[Boo|boo]]!
Taras: Anna! Don't jump out from behind the door!
Mama: Here, everyone. I made hot pancakes.
Taras: [[Mmm|mmm]], they're so good! Now my morning is better.

exclamations.title: Ha-Ha! Movie Night
exclamations.story:
Dad: Look, the dog is wearing Grandpa's hat! [[Ha|ha]]!
Dad: And now he's dancing! [[Ha-ha-ha|ha-ha-ha]]!
Anna: [[Heh|heh]], it's a really funny movie.
Taras: [[Ha-ha|ha-ha]]! I'm sending this part to my friends. I wrote "[[hehe]]."
Sofia: [[Hee-hee|hee-hee]]! The dog fell into the cake!
Grandpa: [[Ho-ho|ho-ho]], what do we have here? A dog in a Santa hat!
Grandpa: [[Ho-ho-ho|ho-ho-ho]]! Merry Christmas, little dog!
Mama: Everyone is laughing. This is our best movie night.

exclamations.title: Stop! Bravo!
exclamations.story:
Max: [[Stop|stop]]! Nobody can go into the castle!
Anna: [[Psst|psst]], Max, you're on the wrong side of the stage.
Teacher: [[Achtung|achtung]], everyone! Just a joke. Now the ship scene, please.
Teacher: [[Basta|basta]]! No more phones on stage.
Taras: [[Mayday|mayday]]! Our plane is falling into the sea!
Anna: We see the plane! Send an [[SOS]] to the coast!
Dad: [[Bravo|bravo]]! What a great show!
Grandma: [[Bravissimo|bravissimo]]! I loved every minute.
Sofia: [[Olé|ole]]! Max, you were the best guard!
Grandpa: [[Vivat|vivat]], young actors!
Max: Thank you! Next time I want to shout "[[banzai]]" like soldiers in old films.

exclamations.title: Meow, Moo, Bam!
exclamations.story:
Anna: Grandma's village is so quiet. I can finally read my book.
Max: Listen, the kitten says "[[meow]]." It wants food.
Anna: And the cow outside says "[[moo]]."
Grandpa: [[Bam|bam]]! Sorry, the wind closed the door.
Max: Now a car is going "[[beep-beep]]" outside the gate.
Anna: And the old clock in the hall goes "[[tick-tack]]."
Grandma: [[La-la|la-la]]... I forgot the words of my song.
Grandma: [[La-la-la|la-la-la]]... [[Tra-la-la|tra-la-la]]! Dinner is ready!
Anna: This village isn't quiet, Grandma, but I love it.

exclamations.title: GG! Game Night
exclamations.story:
Taras: Look at my hero's funny new hat!
Dmytro: [[LOL]], it looks like a banana!
Oleh: [[Kek|kek]], that's the best hat in the game.
Dmytro: Why did the robot cross the road? To charge his phone. [[Bazinga|bazinga]]!
Taras: Oh no, the screen says "[[Game over|game over]]."
Oleh: Good match, everyone. [[GG]]!
Mama: Taras, dinner! All this game talk is just [[blah blah blah]] to me.
Taras: OK, Mama, I'm coming!

exclamations.title: Ciao! Hello Around the World
exclamations.story:
Max: What's in your notebook, Anna?
Anna: Hello and goodbye words from my trips and friends.
Anna: In Italy, people say "[[ciao]]" and "[[arrivederci]]."
Max: And in Mexico?
Anna: "[[Adios|adios]]." My friend from Paris says "[[adieu]]."
Max: What about Hawaii?
Anna: There they say "[[aloha]]." In Japan, I learned "[[konnichiwa]]" and "[[sayonara]]."
Max: And India?
Anna: My yoga teacher says "[[namaste]]." Her mother says "[[namaskar]]."
Max: Cool! Please teach me all of them tomorrow.

exclamations.title: Words of Faith and Peace
exclamations.story:
Anna: This evening of many faiths is lovely, and everyone greets me so warmly.
Mr. Levin: [[Shalom|shalom]], Anna! Welcome to our evening.
Anna: Thank you! Look, there's Amira, my friend from university.
Amira: [[Salaam|salaam]], Anna! I'm so happy you came.
Anna: Will you come to my birthday party next Saturday?
Amira: [[Inshallah|inshallah]], I'll be there with a cake.
Anna: How is your mother? I heard she was sick.
Amira: [[Alhamdulillah|alhamdulillah]], she's much better now.
Max: Listen, the church choir is starting. They're singing "[[Alleluia|alleluia]]."
Anna: And now the "[[Ave|ave]] Maria." It's so beautiful and calm.
Amira: We use different words, but tonight we all wish each other peace.
